title: Research Question to Method Mapper
summary: Read four fictional research questions and decide what kind of claim each is trying to support, what design it implies, and what you would still need to know before choosing an analysis.
learningObjectives: Identify what kind of claim a research question is trying to support before considering any analysis.
Distinguish description, difference, association, prediction, explanation and interpretation as research aims.
Explain why the same kind of number can require different treatment depending on the design that produced it.
Name the further information a method choice depends on, including sampling, allocation, measurement and epistemological position.
Recognise a genuinely ambiguous research question and say what would settle it.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native selects, radios, checkboxes and buttons throughout, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. The research question and a running summary of the learner's reading are pinned to the top of the stage so both stay visible while the four controls are set. Feedback states its standing in words - 'Well supported', 'Defensible', 'Hard to defend from this wording' - so the coloured left border is a redundant cue. Progress through the four questions is shown in a stage track where the current and completed steps are named in visually hidden text as well as marked. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; focus moves to newly revealed headings; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths; forced-colours rules provided. Four representative questions rather than six, and the four decisions appear one at a time: each is revealed once the one before it has an answer, so the chain from aim to design is built rather than presented. Anything held back sits inside a native <details> element, reachable by keyboard in one step and announced as collapsed rather than being disabled.
readmeTopic: Reading a research question: what claim it makes, what design could support it, and what you still need to know
simulationNotes: Four invented research questions with invented settings and sample sizes, selected from the original six to keep one clear instance of each contrast; the two dropped questions (sleep and working memory, forecasting marks) made points the surviving four already carry. There is no score and no single answer key: each option for each question carries a standing of well supported, defensible or hard to defend, with a written note explaining what that reading would commit the researcher to. Part four - what you still need to know - uses a different set of standings: decisive, reasonable, already answered in the description, or not bearing on this question. The fourth question, on group-work disengagement, is deliberately ambiguous, with explanation and interpretation both marked well supported and all three of qualitative, quantitative and mixed defensible, because the wording does not contain the commitment that would settle it. No statistical test is named anywhere in the tool. No real study, dataset, department or researcher is described.
